# BRDF and Relighting Extensions

Also called: Relightable 3D Gaussian Splatting, PBR 3DGS, Inverse Rendering with Gaussians

## Overview
These methods extend standard [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) by decoupling material properties from lighting, enabling physically based rendering (PBR) and dynamic relighting [S1, S2, unofficial]. Unlike standard 3DGS, which bakes view-dependent appearance into [spherical harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) (SH) coefficients under an [emission-absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md), these extensions store explicit BRDF parameters (albedo, roughness, normals) per Gaussian, allowing the scene to be illuminated by arbitrary light sources and environment maps [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D primitives into 2D screen space and accumulating color based on depth order or spatial locality [G].

1.  **Projection:** Primitives are transformed from [world space](#2511-voxel-coordinate-systems-and-conversion.md) to camera space [G].
2.  **Rasterization:** Primitives are assigned to screen tiles [G]. Visibility is determined by bounding boxes or projected extents [G].
3.  **[Compositing](#2436-compositing.md):** Color is accumulated using front-to-back [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) or order-independent techniques [G].
4.  **Sorting:** Most methods require sorting primitives by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back compositing, although some variants use [spatial hashing](#5002-spatial-hashing.md) or cell-level sorting to approximate this or enable order-independent transparency [G].

## Subtopics

### [3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding](1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-brdf-embedding.md)
This method extends standard 3DGS by embedding physically based rendering (PBR) parameters into each Gaussian primitive, enabling per-point BRDF evaluation and relighting. Unlike standard 3DGS, which bakes lighting into spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and assumes an emission-absorption model, this approach decouples material properties from lighting, allowing for specular highlights and [diffuse reflections](#4896-whitted-style-shading-with-diffuse-glossy-materials.md). It distinguishes itself from siblings like [3DGS-DR](1471-3dgs-dr.md) and [Relightable 3D Gaussian](6001-relightable-3d-gaussian.md) by explicitly storing incident lighting and BRDF parameters per Gaussian, facilitating direct lighting reconstruction via environment maps and indirect lighting via SH. See [3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding](1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-brdf-embedding.md).

### [3D Gaussian Splatting with Reflection and Relighting](5873-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-reflection-and-relighting.md)
This method extends standard 3DGS by incorporating classical reflection and shading concepts to address limitations with highly reflective surfaces and enable dynamic relighting. Unlike standard 3DGS, which bakes lighting into spherical harmonics via an emission-absorption model, this approach allows for physically based rendering (PBR) by augmenting Gaussian kernels with environmental information. It leverages the natural normal estimation provided by the shortest axis of the Gaussian kernel to achieve high-quality rendering of reflective objects with training efficiency. See [3D Gaussian Splatting with Reflection and Relighting](5873-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-reflection-and-relighting.md).

### [Relightable 3D Gaussian](6001-relightable-3d-gaussian.md)
[Relightable 3D Gaussian](#6001-relightable-3d-gaussian.md) is a method that extends 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) by assigning per-Gaussian Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) parameters and precomputed visibility to enable dynamic relighting and shadow casting. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling material properties from view-dependent appearance, allowing the scene to be illuminated by arbitrary light sources rather than relying solely on captured environment maps. See [Relightable 3D Gaussian](6001-relightable-3d-gaussian.md).

### [Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR)](6153-inverse-rendering-with-gaussians-gs-ir-gir.md)
[Inverse Rendering with Gaussians](#6153-inverse-rendering-with-gaussians-gs-ir-gir.md) (GS-IR) is a method that recovers physically accurate material and lighting properties from images by optimizing 3D Gaussian primitives. It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which typically assumes fixed, view-dependent colors, by introducing differentiable [shading models](#837-shading-models.md). GS-IR distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding](1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-brdf-embedding.md) by employing a split-sum approximation to handle indirect lighting, allowing for the separation of diffuse and specular components in the optimization process. See [Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR)](6153-inverse-rendering-with-gaussians-gs-ir-gir.md).

### [BRDF Decoder Strategies](8147-brdf-decoder-strategies.md)
[BRDF Decoder Strategies](#8147-brdf-decoder-strategies.md) define how 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives store and interpret surface reflectance properties to enable relighting and [physically-based rendering](#6815-physically-based-rendering-pbr-lighting.md). While standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [3D Gaussian Splatting](52-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) encodes color as a view-dependent spherical harmonic expansion, BRDF decoders map geometric attributes (position, covariance) and material parameters (albedo, roughness, metalness) to a reflectance function. This approach solves the problem of view-independent material representation, allowing for dynamic illumination changes. It differs from [3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding](1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-brdf-embedding.md) by explicitly regressing physical PBR parameters rather than learning implicit embeddings, and from [3D Gaussian Splatting with Reflection and Relighting](5873-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-reflection-and-relighting.md) by focusing on the specific architectural choices (MLP vs. analytical models) for decoding these parameters. See [BRDF Decoder Strategies](8147-brdf-decoder-strategies.md).

#### GaussianShader Material Model
**Definition**
Enhances 3DGS by incorporating trainable material parameters: diffuse $d_p$, specular $s_p$, roughness $\rho_p$, and normal $n_p$, along with a global environment map [S1].

**Formula**
The fused color $c_p$ for a kernel is computed as:
$$ c_p(r_i) = d_p + s_p \odot L_s(r_i, n_p, \rho_p) $$
where $r_i$ is the view direction from camera to pixel $i$, $\odot$ is element-wise multiplication, and $L_s$ is the specular light [S1].

**Parameter**
$L_s(r_i, n_p, \rho_p)$ is the specular light for the kernel along $r_i$ given the normal and roughness. It can be pre-filtered into multiple mip maps [S1].

## Background
The extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting to support PBR and relighting emerged as a solution to the limitation of baked lighting in standard 3DGS. Standard 3DGS uses spherical harmonics to encode view-dependent color, which cannot easily separate material from illumination. Early works like GaussianShader [S1] introduced trainable material parameters to enable basic PBR. Subsequent methods such as Relightable 3D Gaussian and GS-IR expanded this to include shadow casting, inverse rendering, and split-sum approximations for indirect lighting. These techniques are primarily used in computer graphics for virtual production, digital twins, and scene understanding where dynamic lighting is required.
